To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RightSpeed is effective and efficient at reducing energy consumption by dynamically changing speed and voltage to meet performance targets.

(a) PACE can reduce CPU energy consumption 6.1–8.7% for a processor with 5 speed settings and 2 voltage settings, and (b) PACE is effective even when the processor can only run at 2 speeds and 2 voltages, which are the maximum number of settings for the current generation processors.
RightSpeed is a task-based speed/voltage scheduler that is able to meet application performance targets with low overhead and that can save energy on future processors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and evaluation of a task-based scheduler that takes advantage of dynamic processor speed and voltage control to save energy while meeting task deadlines.
how to best use the new processor technologies that are available today and those that will be available in the future.
energy efficiency and performance of computer systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PACE can save energy and that it is a good algorithm for scheduling tasks.
RightSpeed is a good solution for saving energy in Windows 2000, but the extent of its energy savings depends on processor capabilities.
RightSpeed is an effective energy saving scheduler for future processors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RightSpeed is an effective, efficient, and practical energy‐saving technique that can reduce overall energy consumption in the future.
RightSpeed can save energy for future processors and that it can reduce the energy consumed by a processor even if it does not have the ability to run faster.

PACE is the first algorithm to reduce the energy consumed by a CPU by 5.6% relative to the standard algorithm, and that RightSpeed is an efficient implementation of PACE that is suitable for use on real systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability of processors to dynamically change speed or voltage can significantly reduce energy consumption, and that task‐based scheduling is an effective way to use this capability.
the energy consumption of processors is highly controllable by software, and that software can use this controllability to reduce the energy consumption of the processor by up to 8.7%.
it is possible for the operating system to use processor speed and voltage settings to save energy, even without the help of application developers.
